text:
Force five: tariffs and the dollar. In February, the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs.

The average effective US tariff rate fell from fourteen point three percent to ten and a half, then climbed back to almost twelve in April. Before 2025 it was about two and a half.

A temporary global surcharge that replaced them expired on the twenty-fourth of July. Tariffs now come sector by sector.

For you, the bigger story is the currency. In 2025 the euro rose thirteen percent against the dollar. World stocks gained twenty-one percent in dollars, but only seven in euros.

This year it turned. The euro started the year at one seventeen, peaked just above one twenty in January, and is now around one twelve.

About seventy percent of a world ETF is priced in dollars, and the dollar is up almost five percent against the euro since January.

In euros, the M S C I World was up fourteen percent this year to the end of August.

The risk is the reverse. If Trump gets his rate cuts, the dollar would likely fall, and euro investors would give some of that back.

Force six: the midterms, on the third of November. Prediction markets give the Democrats around eighty percent odds of winning the House. The Senate is a toss-up.

Midterm years are usually rough. Since 1950, the S and P five hundred has fallen seventeen and a half percent from peak to trough in the average midterm year, against eleven to thirteen in other years.

This year, the worst fall so far was under ten percent, in March.

And here's the part people forget. In the twelve months after every midterm election since 1946, the S and P five hundred went up. On average, by about sixteen percent.

That's history, not a promise. But it's one reason not to sell before an election.

So what does all this mean if you own a world ETF in euros? Three scenarios, not forecasts.

One: the Fed keeps hiking and yields stay above five percent. Expensive stocks, especially the AI giants, are most at risk, while bonds and cash finally pay.

Two: Trump gets his way and rates fall fast. Stocks may like it at first, but the dollar would likely weaken, and inflation could come back.

Three: Hormuz reopens. Oil falls toward that sixty-nine dollar forecast, inflation cools, and both the Fed and the E C B can stop hiking.

My takeaways, not advice.

One: this is an energy shock. Watch oil and the Strait of Hormuz more than every headline about the Fed.

Two: bonds pay again. Five point three five percent in the US, around two and a half on euro cash and short bonds.

Three: about seventy percent of your world ETF is in dollars. A rate cut that Trump celebrates could cost you on the currency.

Four: since 1946, the year after a midterm has always ended higher. Selling before the vote has been the expensive move.

Which of the six forces worries you most? Tell me in the comments. Sources are in the description, and this isn't financial advice.
